course.title: React + TypeScript Full-Stack Mastery
course.description: A comprehensive 40-part course taking you from absolute beginner to confident full-stack developer using React 18+, TypeScript 5+, and modern tooling. Covers component architecture, hooks, state management with Zustand/Redux, React Router, API integration with TanStack Query, testing with Vitest, and a complete capstone SaaS project.

blocks.value: Understanding React

React is a **declarative**, **component-based** JavaScript library for building user interfaces. Developed by Meta (formerly Facebook) and released in 2013, React introduced the concept of the **Virtual DOM** — a lightweight in-memory representation of the actual DOM that enables efficient UI updates without directly manipulating the browser's DOM tree.

blocks.alt: React logo and component tree visualization
blocks.caption: React's component-based architecture allows you to build complex UIs from small, isolated pieces.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: A clean, modern infographic showing the React logo (atom-like symbol) at the top center, with branching component trees below. Each node is a rounded rectangle representing a component (Header, Sidebar, MainContent, Footer). Arrows show unidirectional data flow. Color palette: React blue (#61DAFB), dark navy background (#282C34), white text. Flat design style with subtle shadows. 16:9 aspect ratio.
Why React + TypeScript?

While React works with plain JavaScript, pairing it with **TypeScript** provides compile-time type safety, better IDE autocomplete, and self-documenting code. TypeScript catches errors before they reach production — a game-changer for large applications. React 18+ has first-class TypeScript support, making the developer experience seamless.

blocks.output: Renders a heading "Hello, [name]!" and optionally displays the age if provided. TypeScript ensures the `name` prop is always a string and `age` is optional.

blocks.value: The Virtual DOM Explained

When state changes, React creates a new Virtual DOM tree, compares it with the previous one using a **diffing algorithm** (reconciliation), and updates only the changed nodes in the real DOM. This minimizes expensive DOM operations and keeps your app fast.

blocks.output: Renders a button showing "Count: 0". Each click increments the number. React efficiently updates only the text node inside the button, not the entire DOM tree.

blocks.question: What is the primary purpose of React's Virtual DOM?
options: To replace the browser's DOM entirely
To minimize direct DOM manipulation for better performance
blocks.explanation: The Virtual DOM is a lightweight copy of the real DOM. React uses it to compare changes and update only the necessary parts of the actual DOM, avoiding expensive full re-renders.

blocks.question: Which of the following are core principles of React? (Select all that apply)
blocks.explanation: React is declarative (you describe what the UI should look like), component-based (UI built from reusable pieces), and uses unidirectional data flow (data flows down via props). Two-way binding is not a React default — it requires explicit handler wiring.

blocks.question: What is the name of the algorithm React uses to compare the new Virtual DOM with the previous one?
blocks.explanation: Reconciliation is React's diffing algorithm that determines the minimal set of changes needed to update the real DOM when state or props change.

blocks.question: In the TypeScript interface `GreetingProps`, what does the `?` symbol indicate for the `age` property?
blocks.explanation: In TypeScript, the `?` symbol after a property name makes it optional. So `age?: number` means the `age` prop can be provided or omitted when using the component.

blocks.question: What does `React.FC<GreetingProps>` signify in the component declaration?
options: It creates a new React context
It defines a functional component with typed props
It registers the component as a forward ref
It enables server-side rendering for the component
blocks.explanation: `React.FC<Props>` is a generic type alias that stands for React Function Component. It types the component's props and automatically includes `children` in the type definition (though modern practice often avoids it).

parts.partTitle: Part 2: Setting Up Your Dev Environment

blocks.value: Creating a React + TypeScript Project

The fastest way to start a modern React + TypeScript project is with **Vite** — a next-generation build tool that provides instant server start and lightning-fast HMR (Hot Module Replacement). Vite replaces the older Create React App (CRA) toolchain and is now the industry standard.

# Create a new React + TypeScript project with Vite
npm create vite@latest my-react-app -- --template react-ts

# Navigate into the project
cd my-react-app

# Install dependencies
npm install

# Start the development server
npm run dev
blocks.output: Vite scaffolds a project with TypeScript configured, creates a `src/` directory with `App.tsx` and `main.tsx`, installs dependencies, and starts a dev server at `http://localhost:5173`.

blocks.alt: VS Code editor with React TypeScript code
blocks.caption: A well-configured IDE with IntelliSense, ESLint, and Prettier dramatically improves your React + TypeScript workflow.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: Screenshot-style mockup of VS Code showing a split view. Left pane: file explorer with `src/components/Button.tsx` highlighted. Right pane: code editor with syntax-highlighted TypeScript React code showing a Button component with typed props. Bottom panel shows terminal with Vite dev server running. Theme: Dark mode (VS Code Dark+). Color accents: React blue for JSX tags, orange for strings, cyan for types. Clean, professional developer workspace aesthetic.
Essential Tooling Configuration

For a professional setup, configure **ESLint** with TypeScript support, **Prettier** for code formatting, and **Path Aliases** for clean imports. These tools catch bugs early and enforce consistent code style across your team.

blocks.output: Enables clean imports like `import { Button } from '@components/Button'` instead of relative paths like `../../../components/Button`. The IDE resolves these automatically.
Vite now recognizes `@/` and `@components/` aliases at build time, bundling the correct files while keeping your import statements clean and refactor-friendly.

blocks.value: Project Structure Best Practices
A well-organized project structure scales with your application. Group by **feature** rather than by file type — this keeps related code together and makes navigation intuitive as your app grows.

my-react-app/
├── src/
│   ├── components/          # Reusable UI components
│   │   ├── Button/
│   │   │   ├── Button.tsx
│   │   │   ├── Button.test.tsx
│   │   │   └── Button.module.css
│   ├── features/            # Feature-specific modules
│   │   └── auth/
│   │       ├── LoginForm.tsx
│   │       └── useAuth.ts
│   ├── hooks/               # Custom React hooks
│   ├── types/               # Shared TypeScript types
│   ├── utils/               # Helper functions
│   ├── App.tsx
│   └── main.tsx
├── public/
├── index.html
├── package.json
├── tsconfig.json
└── vite.config.ts
blocks.output: A scalable project structure where each feature (auth, dashboard, etc.) contains its own components, hooks, and types. This co-location pattern prevents import spaghetti and makes code ownership clear.

blocks.question: Which tool is recommended for scaffolding a modern React + TypeScript project?
blocks.explanation: Vite with the `react-ts` template is the modern standard. It provides faster dev server startup, instant HMR, and a leaner configuration compared to the now-deprecated Create React App.

blocks.question: Which of the following are benefits of using path aliases in a React + TypeScript project? (Select all that apply)
blocks.explanation: Path aliases make imports cleaner (`@components/Button` vs `../../../components/Button`), simplify refactoring (move files without changing imports), and improve IDE support. They do not directly affect build performance.

blocks.question: In the Vite config, which Node.js module is used to resolve absolute paths for aliases?
blocks.explanation: The Node.js `path` module (specifically `path.resolve`) is used to create absolute paths from relative ones, ensuring aliases point to the correct directories regardless of where the config file is located.

blocks.question: What is the recommended project organization strategy for scaling React applications?
options: Group all components in one folder, all hooks in another, all types in another
Group by file type (.tsx, .ts, .css) in separate top-level folders
Group by feature, co-locating related components, hooks, and types
Keep everything in a single src folder with no subdirectories
blocks.explanation: Feature-based organization co-locates related code (components, hooks, types) within feature folders (e.g., `features/auth/`). This scales better than grouping by file type because it keeps related code together and makes navigation intuitive.

blocks.question: What does HMR stand for in the context of Vite's development server?
blocks.explanation: Hot Module Replacement (HMR) allows modules to be updated in the browser at runtime without a full page refresh. Vite provides instant HMR, preserving component state during development.

blocks.value: Understanding JSX and TSX

**JSX** (JavaScript XML) is a syntax extension that lets you write HTML-like code inside JavaScript. **TSX** is the TypeScript version of JSX, giving you the same expressive syntax with full type safety. Under the hood, JSX/TSX compiles to `React.createElement()` calls.

blocks.output: Both snippets produce the same React element object. TSX is syntactic sugar that makes component code readable and declarative while TypeScript enforces type correctness.

blocks.caption: TSX syntax is transformed by the compiler into nested React.createElement() calls that build the Virtual DOM tree.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: A split-screen diagram. Left side: clean TSX code showing a nested component tree (`<Card><Header /><Body /></Card>`). A large curved arrow points to the right side showing the compiled output: nested `React.createElement()` calls forming a tree structure. Each node is color-coded by type (blue for HTML elements, green for components, orange for props). Clean vector illustration style on a light gray background. Labels in monospace font.
JSX Rules and Gotchas

JSX has a few important rules: you must return a **single root element** (or use fragments), use `className` instead of `class`, and wrap JavaScript expressions in curly braces `{}`. All tags must be closed, including self-closing tags like ``.

blocks.output: Renders a card div with dynamic className (includes 'active' when isActive is true), interpolated userName, conditional status text, and an image with a dynamically generated alt attribute. The Fragment (`<>...</>`) avoids adding an unnecessary wrapper element to the DOM.

blocks.value: TypeScript in TSX: Typing JSX Elements

TypeScript provides specific types for JSX. `JSX.Element` represents a single React element, `React.ReactNode` accepts elements, strings, numbers, and arrays — making it the most flexible type for children. Use `React.ReactElement` when you need to be specific about the component type.

blocks.output: Renders a div with class 'wrapper' containing an h1, a p tag, and the number 42 as text. TypeScript ensures only valid ReactNode values are passed as children.

blocks.question: What does TSX compile to under the hood?
blocks.explanation: TSX is syntactic sugar that transpiles to `React.createElement()` calls. These calls return plain JavaScript objects (React elements) that describe what should appear on screen.

blocks.question: Which of the following are valid JSX/TSX rules? (Select all that apply)
options: Use `className` instead of `class` for CSS classes
Wrap JavaScript expressions in curly braces `{}`
Return multiple root elements without a wrapper
Close all tags, including self-closing ones
blocks.explanation: In JSX, you must use `className` (class is a reserved JS keyword), wrap expressions in `{}`, and close all tags. You cannot return multiple root elements without a wrapper (Fragment or container element).

blocks.question: What TypeScript type accepts the widest range of valid React children (elements, strings, numbers, arrays)?
blocks.explanation: `React.ReactNode` is the most inclusive type for children — it accepts JSX elements, strings, numbers, fragments, portals, and arrays of these. `JSX.Element` is more restrictive, only accepting single elements.

blocks.question: What is the purpose of the empty tag syntax `<>...</>` in React?
options: It creates a new HTML5 custom element
It is a React Fragment that groups children without adding extra DOM nodes
It comments out the enclosed JSX
It forces a re-render of the component
blocks.explanation: `<>...</>` is shorthand for `<React.Fragment>...</React.Fragment>`. It allows returning multiple elements from a component without wrapping them in an extra div or other DOM element.

blocks.question: In TSX, why must you use `className` instead of `class` for CSS classes?
options: It is a React convention with no technical reason
`class` is a reserved keyword in JavaScript/TypeScript
TypeScript does not support the `class` attribute
It prevents conflicts with CSS modules
blocks.explanation: `class` is a reserved keyword in JavaScript (used for ES6 classes). JSX/TSX transpiles to JavaScript, so using `class` would cause syntax errors. `className` is the JSX equivalent.

blocks.value: Functional Components in TypeScript

In modern React, **functional components** are the standard. Combined with TypeScript, they provide clear contracts for props, return types, and state. A functional component is simply a function that accepts props and returns JSX.

blocks.output: Renders a button with dynamic CSS class based on the variant prop (e.g., 'btn btn--primary'). TypeScript enforces that label is a string, variant is one of three literal values, and onClick is an optional function. Default values ensure the component works even with partial props.

blocks.alt: Component composition diagram showing parent and child components
blocks.caption: Components compose together like LEGO blocks — each piece is self-contained and reusable.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: An isometric 3D illustration of component composition. A large 'App' block at the top connects downward to medium-sized blocks labeled 'Header', 'Sidebar', 'MainContent'. Each medium block further connects to smaller blocks (e.g., 'MainContent' → 'Card', 'Card' → 'Button', 'Avatar'). Blocks are colored in a cohesive palette (React blue, teal, coral, purple). Connection lines are dotted and animated-looking. Clean, modern flat-3D style on a soft gradient background.
Component Composition with Children

The real power of React lies in **composition** — building complex UIs by nesting simpler components. The `children` prop is the primary mechanism for composition, allowing you to wrap components around content.

blocks.output: Renders an article with a header containing the title, a body with the provided children paragraphs, and a footer with an Edit button. The Card component is reusable with any content passed as children or footer.

blocks.value: Destructuring Props for Clean Code

Destructuring props in the function parameter makes your components more readable. You can also provide default values inline, reducing boilerplate and making the component's interface self-documenting.

blocks.output: Renders a span with classes 'badge badge--green badge--md' containing the text 'New'. Default values ensure the component renders correctly even when optional props are omitted.

blocks.question: What is the primary mechanism for component composition in React?
options: Inheritance from a base Component class
blocks.explanation: The `children` prop is React's primary composition mechanism. It allows components to wrap and render nested content, enabling flexible and reusable component design without inheritance.

blocks.question: Which of the following are benefits of typing props with TypeScript interfaces? (Select all that apply)
options: Compile-time error detection for missing or wrong props
blocks.explanation: TypeScript interfaces provide compile-time checking, IDE autocomplete, and self-documenting code. However, TypeScript types are erased at runtime — they do not provide automatic runtime validation (use PropTypes or Zod for that).

blocks.question: In the Button component, what TypeScript syntax is used to restrict the `variant` prop to only three specific string values?
blocks.explanation: The syntax `'primary' | 'secondary' | 'danger'` is a TypeScript union type. It restricts the prop to exactly those three literal string values, providing both type safety and autocomplete.

blocks.question: Why is destructuring props in the function parameter considered a best practice?
options: It makes the component code cleaner and props immediately visible
blocks.explanation: Destructuring in the parameter list makes the component's props immediately visible at the top of the function, improves readability, and allows setting default values inline. It has no impact on runtime performance or SSR.

blocks.question: What happens if you pass a prop value that is not in the union type to a typed component?
options: The component falls back to a default value
blocks.explanation: TypeScript will show a compile-time error (red squiggly underline in the IDE) if you pass an invalid prop value like `variant='ghost'` when only 'primary', 'secondary', and 'danger' are allowed. This catches bugs before runtime.

blocks.value: Advanced Prop Typing Patterns

As your components grow in complexity, you'll need advanced TypeScript patterns: **optional props**, **union types**, **intersection types**, and **generic components**. These patterns let you build flexible, reusable components with strict type safety.

blocks.output: Renders an alert with dynamic styling based on type. TypeScript enforces that 'error' alerts MUST include an errorCode and title, while 'info' alerts have an optional title, and 'success' alerts have an optional autoDismiss. Invalid prop combinations are caught at compile time.

blocks.alt: TypeScript type system visualization showing union and intersection types
blocks.caption: Discriminated unions let you create components with different prop requirements based on a type discriminator.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: A Venn diagram-style visualization showing TypeScript type operations. Three overlapping circles labeled 'BaseAlertProps', 'InfoProps', 'ErrorProps', 'SuccessProps'. The intersection areas are highlighted in different colors showing how intersection types (`&`) combine properties. Arrows point from a 'type' discriminator to the correct prop shape. Clean vector illustration with TypeScript blue (#3178C6) accents. Monospace font for code snippets embedded in the diagram.
Event Handling with Typed Events

React wraps native DOM events in **SyntheticEvent** objects. TypeScript provides specific event types for different handlers — `React.MouseEvent`, `React.ChangeEvent`, `React.FormEvent`, and more. Using the correct type gives you full autocomplete for event properties.

blocks.output: Renders a form with two controlled inputs. Typing in either field updates the corresponding state property. On submit, the form prevents default browser behavior and logs the form data. TypeScript ensures `e.target` has the correct properties for each event type.

blocks.value: Spreading Props and Rest Parameters

Use the **rest parameter** pattern (`...rest`) to forward unknown props to underlying elements. This is especially useful for wrapper components that need to pass HTML attributes through while adding their own behavior.

blocks.output: Renders a button with a right-positioned arrow icon and the text 'Submit'. All native button attributes (onClick, disabled, type) are forwarded via `...rest`. TypeScript ensures only valid button attributes and IconButton-specific props are accepted.

blocks.question: What TypeScript pattern is used to create components where different variants require different props?
blocks.explanation: Discriminated unions use a common 'type' or 'variant' property to determine which specific props are required. TypeScript narrows the type based on the discriminator value, ensuring correct props for each variant.

blocks.question: Which of the following are valid React event types in TypeScript? (Select all that apply)
blocks.explanation: `React.MouseEvent`, `React.ChangeEvent`, and `React.FormEvent` are all valid React SyntheticEvent types. `React.DOMEvent` is not a valid type — the generic form is `React.SyntheticEvent`.

blocks.question: What TypeScript utility type allows a component to accept all native HTML button attributes plus custom props?
blocks.explanation: Using `interface MyProps extends ButtonHTMLAttributes<HTMLButtonElement>` (or `extends React.ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'>`) allows your component to accept all native button attributes while adding custom ones.

blocks.question: What does the `...rest` pattern achieve in the IconButton component?
options: It creates a new state variable
It forwards all remaining props to the underlying button element
blocks.explanation: The rest parameter (`...rest`) collects all props not explicitly destructured (like icon, iconPosition, children) and spreads them onto the native `<button>` element. This passes through standard HTML attributes like `disabled`, `type`, and `aria-label`.

blocks.question: In the LoginForm, what is the purpose of `e.preventDefault()` in the handleSubmit function?
options: It prevents TypeScript from checking the event type
It stops the form from submitting and reloading the page
It prevents the component from re-rendering
blocks.explanation: `e.preventDefault()` prevents the browser's default form submission behavior (which would cause a full page reload). This allows React to handle the submission with JavaScript, typically sending data to an API without refreshing the page.

blocks.value: Primitive Types and Type Inference

TypeScript's type system builds on JavaScript's primitives: `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `null`, `undefined`, `symbol`, and `bigint`. TypeScript adds **type inference** — when you declare `const name = 'Alice'`, TypeScript automatically infers the type as `string`. Explicit annotations are required for function parameters, empty arrays, and complex objects.

blocks.output: TypeScript infers types for simple declarations. The `greet` function requires string and number parameters and returns a string. The tuple enforces exactly three elements with specific types at each position.

blocks.caption: TypeScript's type system layers on top of JavaScript, adding static analysis without changing runtime behavior.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: A layered cake diagram showing three horizontal layers. Bottom layer: 'JavaScript Runtime' in warm orange. Middle layer: 'TypeScript Compiler (tsc)' in TypeScript blue (#3178C6). Top layer: 'Type Annotations & Interfaces' in teal green. Arrows show data flow: TS code enters the compiler, type errors are caught (shown as red X marks being filtered out), clean JS exits to the runtime. Clean infographic style with subtle gradients. Monospace labels.
Literal Types and Type Narrowing

**Literal types** restrict a variable to a specific value, not just a primitive type. Combined with **union types**, they create powerful enums. Type narrowing uses control flow analysis to refine types within conditional blocks.

blocks.output: `processValue` accepts string or number. Inside the `typeof` check, TypeScript narrows the type to string, so `toUpperCase()` is valid. After the else branch, it's narrowed to number, so `toFixed()` works. The `in` operator narrows union types by checking for property existence.

blocks.value: Type Aliases vs Interfaces

Both `type` and `interface` define object shapes, but they have key differences. **Interfaces** support declaration merging (multiple declarations with the same name are merged), while **type aliases** can represent unions, intersections, and primitives. For React props, interfaces are generally preferred for their extensibility.

blocks.output: The `User` interface is merged to contain both `name` and `age`. The `Status` type alias restricts values to four specific strings. `Admin` extends `User` using interface inheritance. `AdminUser` uses intersection (`&`) to combine types.

blocks.question: What is the key difference between `interface` and `type` in TypeScript?
options: Interfaces support declaration merging; type aliases do not
Type aliases can only describe objects
Interfaces cannot be used for function types
blocks.explanation: Interfaces support declaration merging — multiple declarations with the same name are automatically combined. Type aliases do not support this but can represent unions, intersections, and primitives that interfaces cannot.

blocks.question: Which of the following are valid TypeScript primitive types? (Select all that apply)
blocks.explanation: `string`, `number`, and `boolean` are valid TypeScript primitive types. There is no `char` type in TypeScript — single characters are represented as `string`.

blocks.question: What TypeScript syntax creates a fixed-length array where each position has a specific type?
blocks.explanation: A tuple is defined with syntax like `[string, number, boolean]`, enforcing both the length of the array and the type at each position. This is stricter than a regular array type.

blocks.question: In the `makeSound` function, what TypeScript feature allows the compiler to know `animal` is a `Cat` inside the `if` block?
blocks.explanation: Type narrowing is TypeScript's ability to refine a union type to a more specific type within a conditional block. The `in` operator checks for property existence, allowing TypeScript to narrow `Cat | Dog` to `Cat` inside the if block.

blocks.question: Which syntax combines two types so the resulting type has all properties from both?
blocks.explanation: The intersection operator `&` creates a type that has all properties from both combined types. For example, `type C = A & B` means C has all properties from both A and B.

blocks.value: Defining Object Shapes with Interfaces

Interfaces are the backbone of TypeScript's structural typing system. They describe the shape of objects — what properties exist, their types, and whether they're optional or readonly. In React, interfaces define component props, API responses, and state shapes.

blocks.output: Renders a product card with name, formatted price, optional description, and an Add to Cart button. TypeScript enforces that `id`, `name`, `price`, `sku`, and `onAddToCart` are provided. `sku` and `categories` are readonly — attempting to reassign them causes a compile error.

blocks.alt: Interface structure diagram showing properties and types
blocks.caption: Interfaces act as contracts — they define exactly what an object must contain for TypeScript to accept it.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: A blueprint-style diagram resembling an architectural drawing. A large rectangle labeled 'ProductCardProps' contains labeled compartments for each property: 'id: string' (required, bold border), 'name: string' (required), 'price: number' (required), 'description?: string' (optional, dashed border), 'readonly sku: string' (locked icon), 'onAddToCart: function' (arrow icon). Color-coded by type category. Blueprint grid background in light blue. Technical drawing aesthetic with dimension lines.
Index Signatures and Mapped Types

**Index signatures** let you define objects with dynamic keys. **Mapped types** create new types by transforming properties of an existing type. These are essential for handling dynamic data like form fields, API responses, and configuration objects.

blocks.output: `FormErrors` accepts any string key with a string or undefined value. `PartialUser` uses a mapped type to make all `User` properties optional. TypeScript provides built-in utilities `Partial<T>`, `Readonly<T>`, and `Required<T>` that do the same thing.

blocks.value: Function Types and Method Overloads

TypeScript allows you to type functions precisely — parameters, return types, and even overload signatures for functions that behave differently based on input types. This is crucial for typing callbacks, event handlers, and API functions.

blocks.output: Method overloads let `processInput` have different return types based on the input type. TypeScript correctly infers `result1` as string and `result2` as number. The `ApiClient` interface types async functions that return Promises of typed data.

blocks.question: What does the `readonly` modifier do on an interface property?
options: It prevents the property from being read
It prevents the property from being reassigned after creation
It converts the property to a getter
blocks.explanation: The `readonly` modifier prevents reassignment of a property after the object is created. It does not prevent mutation of nested objects — for deep immutability, you need recursive readonly types.

blocks.question: Which of the following are built-in TypeScript mapped types? (Select all that apply)
blocks.explanation: `Partial<T>` makes all properties optional, `Readonly<T>` makes all properties readonly, and `Required<T>` makes all properties required. There is no built-in `Mutable<T>` type in TypeScript.

blocks.question: What TypeScript syntax allows an object to have any number of string keys with values of a specific type?
blocks.explanation: An index signature like `[key: string]: string` allows an object to have any number of string keys, each with a value of the specified type. This is essential for dynamic data structures like dictionaries and error maps.

blocks.question: In the method overload example, how does TypeScript know `result1` is a string?
options: It reads the function body at compile time
It matches the overload signature for string input
It infers from the variable name
blocks.explanation: TypeScript matches the call to the first overload signature `processInput(input: string): string`. The compiler uses the overload signatures (not the implementation) to determine the return type based on the argument types.

blocks.question: What is the purpose of `keyof User` in a mapped type?
options: It returns the values of all User properties
It creates a union type of all property names as string literals
It checks if a key exists at runtime
It converts the interface to a class
blocks.explanation: `keyof User` produces a union type of all property names in `User` as string literal types (e.g., `'name' | 'email' | 'age'`). This union is used to iterate over properties in mapped types.

blocks.value: Understanding Generics

**Generics** allow you to write reusable, type-safe code that works with multiple types while preserving type information. Instead of using `any`, generics let you parameterize types — like how functions parameterize values. They're essential for building reusable React components and utility functions.

blocks.output: The `identity` function preserves the input type in its return type. `logLength` uses a constraint (`extends { length: number }`) to ensure the generic type has a `length` property. TypeScript rejects calls with types that don't satisfy the constraint.

blocks.caption: Generics act as type variables — they hold a place for a specific type that is determined when the code is used.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: A diagram showing a generic function as a box labeled `identity<T>`. An arrow labeled 'number' points into the box from the left, and an arrow labeled 'number' exits to the right. Below, another flow shows 'string' entering and 'string' exiting. A constraint diagram shows a funnel labeled `extends { length }` filtering out 'number' (shown bouncing off with a red X) while 'string' and 'Array' pass through. Clean vector style with TypeScript blue and green accents. Flowchart aesthetic.
Generic React Components
Generic components are incredibly powerful in React. A generic `List` component can render any type of item while maintaining full type safety for props, callbacks, and render functions.

blocks.output: Renders a ul with two li elements, each containing the user's name and email. TypeScript infers `T` as `User` from the `items` prop, so `renderItem` receives a fully typed `User` object with autocomplete for `name`, `email`, and `id`.

blocks.value: Generic Constraints and Defaults
You can constrain generics to ensure they meet certain requirements, and provide default types for convenience. This is common when building utility hooks and data-fetching components.

blocks.output: The `useApi` hook returns typed data based on the generic parameter. `TResponse` is constrained to object types via `extends Record<string, unknown>`. Default types (`TData = unknown`) mean you can call `useApi()` without specifying generics if you don't need typed data.

blocks.question: What is the primary advantage of using generics over the `any` type?
options: Generics preserve type information and enable autocomplete
Generics require less code to write
blocks.explanation: Generics preserve the specific type information through the function/component, enabling TypeScript to provide autocomplete, type checking, and IntelliSense. `any` bypasses all type checking.

blocks.question: Which of the following are valid ways to use generics in TypeScript? (Select all that apply)
options: Generic type aliases: `type Result<T> = { data: T }`
blocks.explanation: Generics can be applied to functions, interfaces, classes, and type aliases. You cannot declare a generic variable — generics are type parameters, not value parameters.

blocks.question: What TypeScript keyword is used to restrict a generic type parameter to types that have certain properties?
blocks.explanation: The `extends` keyword in generic constraints (e.g., `<T extends { length: number }>`) restricts the generic to types that satisfy the given shape. Only types with the required properties can be used.

blocks.question: In the generic `List<T>` component, how does TypeScript know the type of `user` in the `renderItem` callback?
options: From explicit type annotation on renderItem
By inferring T from the `items` prop
blocks.explanation: TypeScript infers the generic parameter `T` from the `items` prop. Since `items` is `User[]`, TypeScript deduces `T = User`, and therefore the `renderItem` callback receives a `User` parameter.

blocks.question: What does `TData = unknown` mean in `interface ApiResponse<TData = unknown>`?
options: unknown is the default type if no generic is provided
TData is restricted to the unknown type only
It creates a union with unknown
blocks.explanation: The `= unknown` syntax provides a default generic type. If the user calls `useApi()` without specifying `<Post[]>`, `TData` falls back to `unknown`. This makes the generic optional while maintaining type safety.

parts.partTitle: Part 9: Utility Types and Advanced Patterns

blocks.value: Essential Utility Types

TypeScript provides powerful **utility types** that transform existing types. These are indispensable for React development — creating partial state updates, picking specific props, or making properties nullable for forms.

blocks.output: Each utility type transforms `User` in a specific way. `Partial` is perfect for PATCH request payloads. `Pick` creates lightweight types for list views. `Omit` removes auto-generated fields from update forms. `Record` builds dictionaries and lookup maps.

blocks.caption: Utility types are type-level functions — they take a type and produce a new transformed type.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: A factory assembly line diagram showing a base type 'User' entering on a conveyor belt. It passes through transformation stations labeled 'Partial' (makes all dashed/optional), 'Pick' (filters to only 3 properties), 'Omit' (removes 2 properties with a filter), and 'Record' (wraps in a dictionary shape). Each station outputs a differently shaped type block. Industrial/tech aesthetic with TypeScript blue and steel gray colors. Clean vector illustration with labels in monospace font.
Conditional and Template Literal Types

**Conditional types** choose a type based on a condition, similar to ternary operators. **Template literal types** create new string types by combining literals. Together, they enable powerful type-level programming for React prop validation and API typing.

blocks.output: Conditional types evaluate type relationships at compile time. `EventProps` uses key remapping (`as`) to filter only keys starting with 'on'. Template literal types generate all valid combinations of margin utility classes, catching invalid values at compile time.

blocks.value: Type Guards and Assertion Functions

**Type guards** are functions that narrow types at runtime. **Assertion functions** throw errors if conditions aren't met, narrowing types after the call. These patterns are essential for handling API responses and form validation safely.

blocks.output: The `isCat` type guard tells TypeScript that inside the if block, `animal` is narrowed to `Cat`. The `assertIsDefined` function throws if the value is null/undefined, and TypeScript narrows the type to `NonNullable<T>` after the call.

blocks.question: What does `Omit<User, 'id' | 'createdAt'>` produce?
options: A type with only id and createdAt
A type with all User properties except id and createdAt
A union type of id and createdAt
An intersection of User and a new type
blocks.explanation: `Omit<T, K>` creates a new type by removing the specified keys from the original type. It's the opposite of `Pick<T, K>`, which keeps only the specified keys.

blocks.question: Which utility types are useful for React form handling? (Select all that apply)
options: Pick<T, K> for form field subsets
Record<K, V> for field error messages
Exclude<T, U> for removing event types
blocks.explanation: `Partial<T>` is ideal for form state where fields are filled incrementally. `Pick<T, K>` creates types for specific form sections. `Record<string, string>` maps field names to error messages. `Exclude` is less commonly used for forms.

blocks.question: What TypeScript syntax creates a type that is a subset of another type's properties?
blocks.explanation: `Pick<T, K>` constructs a type by picking the set of properties `K` from `T`. For example, `Pick<User, 'name' | 'email'>` creates a type with only the name and email properties from User.

blocks.question: What is the return type annotation `animal is Cat` in a type guard function?
options: A boolean that checks if animal is a Cat instance
A predicate that tells TypeScript to narrow the type
A generic constraint on the animal parameter
A type assertion that casts the value
blocks.explanation: The `is` keyword in a return type (`animal is Cat`) creates a type predicate. When the function returns true, TypeScript narrows the variable's type to `Cat` in the following code block.

blocks.question: What do template literal types like `` `mt-${SpacingToken}` `` enable?
blocks.explanation: Template literal types operate at the type level, not runtime. They generate union types of all valid string combinations, allowing TypeScript to validate string values against patterns at compile time.

parts.partTitle: Part 10: TSX Patterns and Component Typing

blocks.value: Typing React Component Props

Modern React favors typing components without `React.FC` — this avoids implicit `children` typing and gives you full control over the component's interface. Use `ComponentPropsWithoutRef` to inherit native HTML attributes cleanly.

blocks.output: Renders a button with dynamic variant and size classes. `ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'>` inherits all native button attributes. `forwardRef` properly types the ref as `HTMLButtonElement`. The `displayName` aids debugging in React DevTools.

blocks.caption: Properly typed components with forwardRef and HTML attribute inheritance create robust, reusable UI primitives.

blocks.value: IMAGE TYPE: A code editor mockup showing a TypeScript React component file. The left margin shows type hints and IntelliSense tooltips. A Button component is shown with `forwardRef` highlighted. A popup shows the inferred type: `forwardRef<HTMLButtonElement, ButtonProps>`. Arrows point from `ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'>` to a list of inherited attributes (onClick, disabled, type, etc.). Clean dark theme with syntax highlighting. Professional IDE screenshot aesthetic.
Polymorphic Components with as Prop

**Polymorphic components** change their rendered element via an `as` prop while maintaining type safety. A `Text` component can render as `p`, `span`, `h1`, or any other element, inheriting the correct attributes for each.

blocks.output: The `Text` component renders as different HTML elements based on the `as` prop. TypeScript correctly infers available props for each element — `href` is only valid when `as='a'`, `onClick` when `as='button'`, etc. The default element is `span`.

blocks.value: ComponentProps and HTML Attribute Types

TypeScript provides `ComponentProps`, `ComponentPropsWithRef`, and `ComponentPropsWithoutRef` to extract prop types from any React component or HTML element. This is invaluable for wrapper components and HOCs.

blocks.output: Renders a label, an input inheriting all native HTML input attributes, and an optional error message. `ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'input'>` provides types for all standard input attributes (value, onChange, placeholder, etc.) without the ref.

blocks.question: Why is `ComponentPropsWithoutRef<'button'>` preferred over `React.ButtonHTMLAttributes<HTMLButtonElement>`?
options: It excludes the ref prop, preventing type conflicts with forwardRef
It is the only type that works with Vite
blocks.explanation: `ComponentPropsWithoutRef` intentionally excludes the `ref` prop. When using `forwardRef`, you manage the ref separately. Including ref in props would create a type conflict since forwardRef handles ref differently.

blocks.question: Which of the following are valid uses of TypeScript's ComponentProps utilities? (Select all that apply)
options: Extracting props from HTML elements like 'input'
Extracting props from custom React components
Creating wrapper components that inherit native attributes
blocks.explanation: `ComponentProps` and `ComponentPropsWithoutRef` extract prop types from both HTML elements and custom components. They're ideal for wrapper components. They are not used for defining state types — `useState` uses its own generic parameter.

blocks.question: What React hook/utility is used to forward refs to DOM elements while preserving type safety?
blocks.explanation: `forwardRef` is a React utility that lets components pass a ref through to a child DOM element. When combined with `ElementRef<'element'>` and proper generic typing, it maintains full type safety for the ref.

blocks.question: In the polymorphic `Text` component, what does `T extends ElementType = 'span'` mean?
options: T must be a span element only
T must be a valid React element type, defaulting to 'span' if not specified
T is optional and can be any string
T creates a new element type at runtime
blocks.explanation: `T extends ElementType` constrains T to valid React element types (HTML tags or components). The `= 'span'` provides a default value, so if `as` is omitted, the component renders as a span.

blocks.question: What is the purpose of `Omit<ComponentPropsWithoutRef<T>, 'as' | 'children'>` in the polymorphic component?
options: It removes the as and children props from the inherited type
It makes as and children required props
It converts as and children to readonly
It adds as and children to the type
blocks.explanation: `Omit` removes specified keys from a type. We remove 'as' and 'children' because they are explicitly defined in our `PolymorphicProps` type. Without Omit, they'd be defined twice, causing a type error.
